title: The Most Beautiful Roof in the World: Exploring the Rainforest Canopy
author: Kathryn Lasky
source: The Most Beautiful Roof in the World (Harcourt Brace & Co., 1997)
citation: Lasky, Kathryn. The Most Beautiful Roof in the World: Exploring the Rainforest Canopy. Photographs by Christopher G. Knight, Gulliver Green / Harcourt Brace & Co., 1997.

sections.heading: Dr. Meg Lowman and The Eighth Continent

epigraph.quote: To Meg Lowman, the rainforest canopy is not merely the top of the trees; it is an undiscovered world where half of all life on Earth lives.
epigraph.attribution: —Kathryn Lasky, The Most Beautiful Roof in the World

paragraphs: For centuries, rainforest scientists could only study the forest floor—a dark, humid world where less than two percent of sunlight filters through the dense vegetation. But Dr. Margaret 'Meg' Lowman, pioneering field biologist and ecologist, was fascinated by what lay high above: the canopy, towering one hundred and fifty feet into the air. Ecologists call this treetop realm the 'eighth continent' because it contains fifty percent of all plant and animal species on Earth.

To enter this perilous high-altitude ecosystem, Meg invented ingenious tools: rigging mountain-climbing ropes over sturdy mahogany branches, strapping on harnesses, and designing suspended aerial walkways and inflatable tree-top rafts. Suspended in midair, she conducts meticulous research on herbivory—how insects feed on leaves—and documents the incredible biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest.

sections.heading: Canopy Biodiversity: Bromeliads, Tree Vipers, and Leafcutter Ants

epigraph.quote: A single tank bromeliad perched in the crotch of a giant kapok tree is a miniature universe, home to tadpoles, beetles, and microscopic crabs.
epigraph.attribution: —Kathryn Lasky, The Most Beautiful Roof in the World

paragraphs: Climbing with her two young sons, Edward and James, Meg demonstrates that the canopy is buzzing with constant ecological activity. Giant kapok and fig trees are loaded with epiphytes—'air plants' like orchids and bromeliads that grow without touching soil, drawing nutrients directly from rain and mist. A single large bromeliad holds gallons of water, creating an aerial aquarium where poison dart frogs lay eggs and tree vipers hunt.

Meg tracks leafcutter ants carrying green leaf segments twice their weight up ninety-foot trunks to feed underground fungus gardens, and observes how sloths camouflage themselves with green algae in their fur. Through her field journals and public education, Meg teaches that destroying the rainforest canopy wipes out fragile biological webs that regulate global climate and hold potential cures for human diseases.
